minutes.headline: Committee unanimously ratified a one-year paraprofessional contract with a modest raise, deferring pay-scale changes.
minutes.summary: The School Committee opened its 2024-25 year with reports on hiring, the state funding-formula advocacy effort, and a presentation from a proposed new education-foundation nonprofit called Leaf. Most of the meeting concerned the FY26 budget outlook and staff retention crisis, a draft capital plan ranking, and concerns about a proposed town financial-policies manual; the committee also ratified a one-year paraprofessional union contract by roll-call vote and voted to enter executive session on non-union personnel negotiations.

what_happened.line: The committee unanimously ratified a one-year paraprofessional union contract by roll-call vote, with a modest raise and pay-scale changes left for later talks.
The superintendent said the paraprofessional and teacher contracts, health insurance, and the bus contract bid remain unresolved and will shape the FY26 school budget.
The committee voted to approve its priority ranking for the FY26 draft capital plan, topped by the primary school driveway, cited as a bus-time safety hazard.
Members voted to relay concerns about the town's draft financial-policies manual, particularly a grant pre-approval requirement, to the interim town manager rather than act further now.

why_it_matters: The paraprofessional contract affects classroom support staffing and pay heading into a budget year the district already calls tight for retention.
Several open items -- contracts, insurance, and busing -- still have to be settled before the FY26 school budget residents will vote on is finalized.
The capital plan ranking sets which facility and safety projects, including the primary school driveway, the town will be asked to fund first.
watch_next: Pay-scale restructuring for paraprofessionals, to be negotiated separately from this one-year contract.
The October 16 meeting, where strategy, MCAS-based goals, and superintendent goals return to the agenda.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree on every dollar figure and vote outcome that both happened to capture, but each preserves things the other drops entirely: the official minutes hold seven procedural/strategic decisions our minutes never mention are omitted from the official record, while the official minutes add two capital-plan cost lines and several attendee names our captions never resolved. Two things need a human check before either is trusted: the paraprofessional roll-call count (ours says 6-0 with named voters, official just says "all approve" and calls out only Terenzini), and the town-manager recruiting-firm transfer, which is $115,000 in our minutes versus $15,000 in the official text — a large enough gap that it should be checked against the finance committee/select board transfer vote rather than assumed to be a caption slip.
